title: Distributed Rate Limiter
brief: Design a limiter that caps how many requests each client can make, across a fleet of many servers. A client that goes over gets a clear 429 answer. The check must be cheap, because it runs before every request. The single-process algorithms (token bucket, windows) are covered in the LLD Rate Limiter. This page is about doing it across machines.

functional: Limit requests per client key (API key, user or IP) per rule, such as 100 per minute.
Different rules per endpoint and per plan, changeable without a deploy.
Reject excess requests with 429 and a Retry-After header.
Tell every caller how much budget is left, using response headers.
Work the same no matter which gateway a request lands on.

nonFunctional.name: Added latency
nonFunctional.target: The check adds under 2 ms at the 99th percentile

nonFunctional.name: Accuracy
nonFunctional.target: Within a few percent of the limit; never block a client far under its limit

nonFunctional.name: Availability
nonFunctional.target: A limiter failure must not take the API down

nonFunctional.name: Scale
nonFunctional.target: Hundreds of thousands of checks per second, millions of keys

outOfScope: The counting algorithms themselves (see the LLD Rate Limiter)

estimate.note: Assumptions, not facts. The key question: how many operations does the central store see? Checking on every request costs one operation each. Batching only helps when the same keys repeat within one sync interval.

api.does: Internal call from gateway code. Updates the counter and returns the verdict with remaining budget and reset time.
Sent on every response so well-behaved clients can pace themselves.

evolution.title: Counters inside one gateway
evolution.problem: Start with the simplest thing that works: one gateway counts requests per key in a local map and rejects the extra ones.
evolution.change: Use a token bucket or window per key, in memory. Fast and exact, because only one process ever counts.

evolution.title: Central counter, atomic
evolution.problem: With 20 gateways, each counts its own share. A key limited to 100 a minute can send 100 to each gateway, so 2000 get through. Sticky routing breaks when a gateway dies or the key spreads.
evolution.change: Keep one counter per key in a shared store. Update it with a single atomic operation: an increment with expiry, or a small server-side script. A plain read then write lets two gateways read 99 and both allow the 100th.
evolution.numbers: the estimator: one store operation per request

evolution.title: Local counters, batched sync
evolution.problem: Every request now pays a network hop, about a millisecond, and the store sees all of the traffic. At 200K requests per second that is several store nodes, and a slow store slows the API.
evolution.change: Each gateway counts locally and sends its deltas to the store every second, then reads back the global total. It can overshoot the limit slightly between syncs. You trade a little accuracy for latency and load.

evolution.title: Rules as pushed config
evolution.problem: Limits differ per plan and endpoint, and they change during incidents. Redeploying gateways to change a number is too slow.
evolution.change: A rules service holds the limits. It pushes new versions to every gateway, which keep a copy in memory and keep working with the last version if the service is down.

evolution.title: Regions with their own stores
evolution.problem: A gateway in another continent that calls one central store pays 100 ms or more per sync, and the store becomes a cross-ocean dependency.
evolution.change: Each region has its own store. Regions merge counts asynchronously. Each region may spend its share of the limit, so a global limit is approximate by the merge delay.

evolution.title: Catch abuse across many keys
evolution.problem: An attacker rotates through thousands of IPs. Each one stays under its per-key limit, so the limiter never fires, while the total hurts you.
evolution.change: Gateways report their busiest keys to a detector that looks for patterns across keys, then writes block entries and tighter rules back through the rules service. Limits are also stacked: per account, per IP and per network range.

steps.say: A client sends a request with its API key.
The load balancer picks any gateway. They are all equal.
The gateway builds the key (rule, client, window) from its in-memory rules. Rules arrived by push earlier, so no lookup is needed.
It checks the local counter first. If the local count plus the last known global count is under the limit, the request is allowed with no network call.
Every second the gateway sends its count deltas to the store and reads back the global totals.
The request is forwarded. The response carries RateLimit-Remaining and RateLimit-Reset.
A client has used up its budget for this window and sends another request.
Gateway B sees the local plus global count is at the limit.
It rejects at once. The backend never sees the request, which is the point.
The reply is 429 with Retry-After set to the seconds left in the window. The client should wait that long, plus some random jitter.
Meanwhile gateways report their busiest keys to the detector, which sees this key still hammering.
It asks the rules service for a block entry. The new version is pushed to every gateway.

deepDives.title: Exact or approximate counting
deepDives.question: Do we ask the central store on every request, or count locally and sync?

options.name: Central check per request
options.pros: Exact. Simple to reason about. One atomic operation decides.
options.cons: A network hop on every request and the store sees all traffic. A store hiccup is a latency hiccup.

options.name: Local counters, periodic sync
options.pros: No hop on the hot path. Store load drops with batching.
options.cons: Can overshoot by roughly the traffic of one interval across all gateways.

options.name: Leased slices of the budget
options.pros: A gateway reserves a chunk of tokens from the store and spends it locally. Overshoot is bounded by the leases.
options.cons: Unused leased tokens are stranded. Small limits split badly across many gateways.

deepDives.pick: Local counters for high limits, central check for low ones
deepDives.because: A limit of 10,000 per minute can tolerate 2% error and should be fast. A limit of 3 password tries must be exact, so pay the hop. Choose per rule, not for the whole system.

deepDives.title: Fail open or fail closed
deepDives.question: The counter store is unreachable. Do we let requests through or block them?

options.name: Fail open
options.pros: The API stays up. Users never notice a limiter problem.
options.cons: There is no protection while the store is down. Abuse and runaway clients get through.

options.name: Fail closed
options.pros: Protection stays on. Safe for costly or sensitive actions.
options.cons: A limiter outage becomes a full outage. The protection layer is now a single point of failure.

options.name: Degrade to local limits
options.pros: Each gateway keeps enforcing its own share, so there is still a rough cap.
options.cons: Less accurate, and a client spread across gateways may exceed the real limit.

deepDives.pick: Local fallback; fail closed for sensitive rules
deepDives.because: Availability matters more than precision for most APIs. Set failMode per rule: login and SMS-sending stay closed, ordinary reads fall back to local counting.

deepDives.title: Where the limiter lives
deepDives.question: At the edge gateway, as middleware in each service, or as a library?

options.name: API gateway
options.pros: One place. Bad traffic never reaches services. Easy to keep consistent.
options.cons: Only sees the request, not the cost inside. Limits cannot depend on deep service state.

options.name: Middleware in each service
options.pros: Knows the real cost, such as expensive queries. Each team owns its limits.
options.cons: Many copies to keep consistent. Rejected requests have already used a connection.

options.name: Sidecar or shared library
options.pros: Reusable and close to the service, with local state per instance.
options.cons: Versioning across languages and teams. Rollouts are slow.

deepDives.pick: Gateway for coarse, middleware for costly calls
deepDives.because: The gateway protects everything cheaply. Services add their own limits where cost depends on what the call does. Both use the same rules service and counter store.

deepDives.title: What to key on
deepDives.question: Per IP, per account, or something else? How do we stop abuse spread over many IPs?

options.name: Per IP
options.pros: Works before login. Needs no identity.
options.cons: Many users share one IP (offices, mobile carriers). Attackers rotate IPs cheaply.

options.name: Per account or API key
options.pros: Fair per customer. Hard to dodge once authenticated.
options.cons: Useless before login and when accounts are free to create.

options.name: Layered keys plus a detector
options.pros: Limit by key, account and network range. A detector spots patterns across keys.
options.cons: More counters to store. Needs tuning to avoid blocking honest bursts.

deepDives.because: No single key covers all attackers. Cheap per-key limits stop the common case, and the detector deals with distributed abuse using the same store.

failures.impact: Gateways cannot sync. Either everything is blocked or nothing is limited.
failures.fix: Per-rule failMode. Default to local counting with the last known totals. Run replicas, and alert when gateways are on fallback.

failures.impact: A single counter takes all the writes of a giant client and its store shard saturates.
failures.fix: Split the counter into a few sub-counters that are summed on read, or give hot keys local-only counting with a lease.

failures.impact: A typo sets a limit of 1 per minute and blocks every customer within seconds.
failures.fix: Validate rules, roll out by percentage, keep the last good version, and add a global kill switch that sets the limiter to log-only.

failures.impact: Everyone gets Retry-After: 1 and returns at the same instant, creating a spike each second.
failures.fix: Add jitter to Retry-After and document backoff. Use a sliding window so budget returns gradually instead of all at the window edge.

failures.impact: Two gateways read 99, both write 100, and the limit is exceeded.
failures.fix: Do the update in the store as one atomic step: an increment that returns the new value, or a script that checks and increments together. Set the expiry in the same step, so a crash cannot leave a key that never expires.

scaling.limit: One store node tops out at around 100K operations per second
scaling.lever: Shard counters by key with consistent hashing, so one key always lives on one shard. Batch local deltas to cut operations.
Expire counters with their window and keep only recent keys. Use a compact key and a small integer value.
Give each region a share of the budget and merge asynchronously. Accept a small overshoot, or split the limit per region up front.

recap.key: One atomic counter per key beats counting per gateway, and local counters synced in batches keep the hop off the hot path at the cost of a small overshoot.
recap.numbers: 200K requests per second means 200K store operations per second if you check each time, about 2 nodes. With local batching it drops to around 40K. Counters for 10M keys need about 2 GB.
moves: Count in a shared store with an atomic increment, never read then write
Count locally and sync every second to avoid a hop per request
Push rules as versioned config; fail open or closed per rule
Return 429 with Retry-After, and catch many-IP abuse with a detector
